⚡ Module 4 • Asynchronous JavaScript

Learn Asynchronous JavaScript Without Getting Lost in Time

Asynchronous JavaScript is one of the most important, and most confusing, topics in modern development. It matters because real programs wait for things all the time: network requests, timers, files, database calls, API responses, and user input. This page explains why JavaScript is single-threaded, what that means for your code, how callbacks work, why they turn into callback hell, how Promises improve the story, and how async/await makes the same idea easier to read. The tutorial follows the supplied module content closely, but also fills in the extra mental models students usually need before the topic finally clicks.

The one idea everything builds on

Async JavaScript means “do this later without blocking”, not “spin up a new thread”

The module slides say it clearly: JavaScript is single-threaded. That means only one piece of normal JavaScript code is actively running on the main call stack at a time. So when learners first meet setTimeout, Promises, or await, the big surprise is this: JavaScript can stay responsive without creating a new thread for every delay. Instead, the runtime keeps track of future work and feeds it back in when the current work is done.

1. Call Stack

This is the code running right now. JavaScript executes one stack frame at a time.

main() verify()

2. Timers / APIs

Functions like setTimeout wait outside the stack until they are ready.

timer 20ms

3. Queue

When delayed work finishes waiting, its callback joins a queue. It still must wait its turn.

callback()

4. Event Loop

The event loop keeps checking whether the stack is empty and whether the next task can run.

check move run

Simple memory trick: synchronous code runs now, async code is scheduled for later, and the event loop helps decide when “later” happens.

QUIZ ALERT

A classic wrong answer is: “setTimeout creates another thread.” A much better answer is: “setTimeout schedules a callback that the event loop will run later, after the current synchronous work is finished.”

Why JavaScript was designed this way

Single-threaded JavaScript supports responsive user interfaces

JavaScript was born in the browser. Browsers needed a scripting language that could react to clicks, form input, animation, and page events without making page scripting wildly complex. A single main thread keeps DOM updates and most application logic simpler and safer. You do not usually worry about two different JavaScript threads changing the same button at the exact same moment.

Benefit 1: simpler mental model

Most student code can be understood as one line after another, without race-condition thinking being the default.

Benefit 2: safer UI interaction

Having one main thread makes many interface updates more predictable than a “many threads touching the page” design.

Tradeoff: waiting must be non-blocking

Since JavaScript should stay responsive, it needs tools like callbacks, Promises, and the event loop to avoid freezing while waiting.

The “professor explaining the board” moment This body image reinforces the main sequence students should remember: callback → Promise → async/await, all resting on the event loop.
Part 1

Callbacks are the first form of async thinking

A callback is just a function you hand to another function so it can call you back later. In the supplied materials, the fake network example checks whether a username is known. The important thing to notice is not just the syntax. It is the timing.

The callback-based function 
const KNOWN_USERS = ["alice", "bob", "carol"];

function verifyCredentialsCallback(username, callback) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    if (KNOWN_USERS.includes(username)) {
      callback(null, { username, verified: true });
    } else {
      callback(new Error(`Unknown user: ${username}`));
    }
  }, 20);
}

What students should notice

  • verifyCredentialsCallback finishes quickly and returns immediately.
  • The timer delays the real answer.
  • The callback follows the Node pattern callback(error, result).
  • On success, error is null. On failure, the error arrives first.
Plain-English translation “Start the verification now. I know you cannot answer immediately. When you are done, call this function and tell me whether it worked.”
A single callback in use 
console.log("Checking alice...");

verifyCredentialsCallback("alice", (err, result) => {
  if (err) {
    console.log("Error:", err.message);
    return;
  }

  console.log("Verified:", result.username);
});

console.log("This line runs BEFORE the callback above");

// Output:
// Checking alice...
// This line runs BEFORE the callback above
// Verified: alice

Why the output order matters

The line after the async call runs before the callback result. This is the first big “aha” moment in asynchronous JavaScript. Many students expect the program to stop and wait. But if it did that for every network call, web pages and servers would feel frozen and unresponsive.

Key sentence: the function call starts the work now, but the result arrives later.

Callback hell 
verifyCredentialsCallback("alice", (err1, result1) => {
  if (err1) {
    console.log("Error:", err1.message);
    return;
  }

  console.log("Verified:", result1.username);

  verifyCredentialsCallback("bob", (err2, result2) => {
    if (err2) {
      console.log("Error:", err2.message);
      return;
    }

    console.log("Verified:", result2.username);

    verifyCredentialsCallback("dave", (err3, result3) => {
      if (err3) {
        console.log("Error:", err3.message);
        return;
      }

      console.log("Verified:", result3.username);
    });
  });
});

Callback hell, explained simply

  • Every next step is nested inside the previous step.
  • The code drifts further and further right.
  • Each layer needs its own error check.
  • The main logic becomes hard to see.

This is why people started wanting a flatter, cleaner abstraction. The async problem did not go away. The code just needed a better way to describe it.

Part 2

Promises package the future result into an object you can work with

A Promise is a placeholder for a value you do not have yet. That value may eventually succeed or fail. So instead of handing a callback directly into the function, the function returns a Promise and your code reacts to it.

The Promise-based function 
function verifyCredentials(username) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      if (KNOWN_USERS.includes(username)) {
        resolve({ username, verified: true });
      } else {
        reject(new Error(`Unknown user: ${username}`));
      }
    }, 20);
  });
}

The Promise vocabulary

  • Pending: still waiting.
  • Resolved / fulfilled: succeeded with a value.
  • Rejected: failed with an error.
  • resolve(value) moves to success.
  • reject(error) moves to failure.
Best beginner analogy Think of a restaurant pager. You do not have the food yet. You have a device that represents the future result. When the food is ready, the pager leads you to the result.
Chaining .then() and .catch() 
verifyCredentials("alice")
  .then((result) => {
    console.log("Verified:", result.username);
    return verifyCredentials("bob");
  })
  .then((result) => {
    console.log("Verified:", result.username);
    return verifyCredentials("dave");
  })
  .then((result) => {
    console.log("Verified:", result.username);
  })
  .catch((err) => {
    console.log("Error:", err.message);
  });

// Output:
// Verified: alice
// Verified: bob
// Error: Unknown user: dave

Why Promises feel better than nested callbacks

  • The code reads more like a straight line.
  • .then() handles the next successful step.
  • .catch() can catch an error from any earlier Promise in the chain.
  • The “story” of the code becomes easier to follow.
Promise.all for concurrent independent work 
Promise.all([
  verifyCredentials("alice"),
  verifyCredentials("bob"),
  verifyCredentials("carol"),
]).then((results) => {
  console.log(results.map((r) => r.username));
});

// Output:
// [ 'alice', 'bob', 'carol' ]

When is Promise.all the right choice?

Use it when each async task is independent. Checking alice, bob, and carol does not require one result before starting the next, so all three can start together.

  • Everything starts immediately.
  • The result arrives when all succeed.
  • If one fails, the whole Promise rejects.

Important nuance

In classroom conversation, people often say Promise.all runs things “in parallel.” That is useful shorthand. More precisely, it starts multiple asynchronous operations without waiting for each one in sequence.

Part 3

async/await is still Promise-based, but it reads more like normal code

One of the biggest breakthroughs for learners is realizing that async/await is not a separate universe. It is Promise logic with friendlier syntax. Under the hood, the Promise model is still there.

Sequential async/await 
async function checkLogins() {
  try {
    const alice = await verifyCredentials("alice");
    console.log("Verified:", alice.username);

    const bob = await verifyCredentials("bob");
    console.log("Verified:", bob.username);

    const dave = await verifyCredentials("dave");
    console.log("Verified:", dave.username);
  } catch (err) {
    console.log("Error:", err.message);
  }
}

What await actually does

  • await can only be used inside an async function, or modern top-level module contexts.
  • It pauses that async function until the Promise settles.
  • It does not freeze the entire JavaScript program.
  • You can use ordinary try/catch for failure handling.

Best mental model: await means “pause this function here until the future result arrives.”

await with Promise.all 
async function checkAllLogins() {
  const results = await Promise.all([
    verifyCredentials("alice"),
    verifyCredentials("bob"),
    verifyCredentials("carol"),
  ]);

  console.log(results.map((r) => r.username));
}

Readable and fast

This is a great real-world pattern. You still launch independent work together with Promise.all, but you read the final line with the cleaner await style.

  • Sequential await: best when step 2 depends on step 1.
  • await Promise.all(...): best when jobs are independent.
Promise.allSettled for “show me every result” 
async function checkConcurrently(usernames) {
  const results = await Promise.allSettled(
    usernames.map((username) => verifyCredentials(username))
  );

  for (const result of results) {
    if (result.status === "fulfilled") {
      console.log("Verified:", result.value.username);
    } else {
      console.log("Error:", result.reason.message);
    }
  }
}

Why Promise.allSettled matters

Sometimes you do not want one failure to destroy the entire batch. In the lab, one username is deliberately unknown. If you need to report every success and every failure, Promise.allSettled is a better fit than Promise.all.

The event loop

The event loop is the traffic controller that makes the model work

Students often hear “event loop” as a mysterious phrase. But it becomes easier if you treat it as a manager checking whether JavaScript is free to take the next task.

Microtask vs timer demonstration 
console.log("1. Start");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("4. Timer callback");
}, 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("3. Promise callback");
});

console.log("2. End");

// Output:
// 1. Start
// 2. End
// 3. Promise callback
// 4. Timer callback

Try the demo

Click "Run Demo" to see the order.

Promise callbacks run before timer callbacks in this example because Promise reactions go into the microtask queue, which is processed before the regular task queue used by timers.

Advanced but helpful

You do not need to memorize every detail of the browser or Node runtime to succeed in this module, but it helps to know that not all queues are identical. Promise callbacks are treated with higher priority than timer callbacks.

Things students often get wrong

Common mistakes and the better answers

Use this section as a last-minute review sheet.

Mistake Why it is wrong Better thinking
“setTimeout runs exactly when the delay ends.” The delay only makes the callback eligible to run. It still waits until the current stack is done and the event loop can run it.
“await blocks the whole program.” It pauses only the current async function. Other events and async work can still continue.
“Promise means success.” A Promise can succeed or fail. Think of it as a future result, not a guaranteed success.
“Promise.all is always best.” If tasks depend on each other, concurrency is not correct. Use Promise.all for independent work only.
“If I forget await, JavaScript will figure it out.” You may be holding a Promise object rather than the real value. Always ask yourself: do I have the value, or do I still have a Promise?
A tiny but important pitfall

Forgetting await is one of the easiest async bugs to write

Many bugs happen because students think they already have data, when they really just have a Promise.

Forgetting await 
async function loginFlow() {
  const tokenPromise = fetch("/login");
  console.log(tokenPromise); // This is a Promise, not the real response yet

  const response = await tokenPromise;
  const data = await response.json();
  console.log(data);
}

What goes wrong here?

fetch("/login") returns immediately with a Promise. If you log that first variable, you do not see the response body. You see a Promise object. Only after await do you get the actual response.

Simple learner rule If a function returns a Promise, treat it like a future answer. Use await or .then() before acting like you already have the data.
Practice and teaching checks

Questions students should be able to answer after this page

These are strong comprehension checks because they test both the idea and the reasoning behind it.

Challenge 1

Why does the line after an async function call often run before the callback or Promise result?

Reveal answer Because the async operation starts now but finishes later. JavaScript keeps moving through the synchronous lines instead of blocking.

Challenge 2

When is sequential async work the correct choice?

Reveal answer When each step depends on the previous step. For example, log in first, then use the returned token to call a protected API.

Challenge 3

What is the real difference between Promises and async/await?

Reveal answer Mostly the syntax and readability. async/await is built on Promises and does not replace the underlying model.

Challenge 4

Why might Promise.allSettled be better than Promise.all in a reporting tool?

Reveal answer Because Promise.allSettled returns every result, including failures, while Promise.all stops with a rejection when one member fails.
Module summary

What students absolutely need to remember

If these points are clear, the whole module becomes manageable.

1. JavaScript is single-threaded in the model taught here

Async work is coordinated through the runtime and event loop, not by spawning a Java-style thread for every delayed operation.

2. Callbacks came first

They work, but nested callbacks become hard to read and hard to maintain.

3. Promises flatten the pyramid

.then() and .catch() let you describe delayed work more cleanly.

4. Promise.all starts independent work together

It is the right choice when tasks do not rely on one another.

5. async/await improves readability

It pauses the current async function until the Promise settles and uses normal try/catch.

6. “Later without blocking” is the master phrase

That sentence ties together callbacks, Promises, async/await, and the event loop.
